chunks: Al-Fadl ibn Shadhan narrated, it was reported from Hanan, who said: 'I was sitting with Suwayd ibn Ghaflah when a man came to him and asked him about a daughter, a wife, and mawali (clients). He said: I will inform you of the ruling of Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) regarding this: He gave the daughter one-half, the wife one-eighth, and what remained he returned to the daughter, and he gave the mawali nothing. Al-Fadl said: And this report is more authentic than what was reported by Salamah ibn Kuhayl, who said: I saw the wife whom Ali (peace be upon him) inherited from, and he gave the daughter one-half and the mawali one-half.'
Because Salamah did not meet Ali (peace be upon him), whereas Suwayd had met Ali (peace be upon him).

He said: As for what was reported: 'That a mawla of Hamz (peace be upon him) died and the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) gave the daughter of Hamz one-half and gave the mawali one-half.' It is a disconnected hadith; it is only from Abdullah ibn Shaddad from the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), and it is mursal (disconnected at the companion level).
He said: And perhaps that was before the descent of the inheritance shares (al-fara'idh), so it was abrogated.
For Allah has prescribed for the allies (al-hulafa') in His Book, saying, Exalted and Great is He: 'And those whose oaths you have made, give them their share.'
So the inheritance shares abrogated all of that with His Exalted saying: 'And those of kinship are closer to one another in the decree of Allah.'
And Ibrahim al-Nakha'i - rejected this hadith regarding the inheritance of the mawla of Hamz - and the correct ruling from this chapter has been clarified by us.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the inheritance of mawali (clients) in Shia jurisprudence according to Ali ibn Abi Talib?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi evaluates the inheritance of a daughter, wife, and mawali by contrasting two reports, ultimately preferring the narration from Suwayd ibn Ghaflah—who directly witnessed Ali’s ruling—over that of Salama ibn Kuhayl. The text argues that the Prophetic practice of granting shares to mawali was abrogated by the Quranic verses on inheritance, which establish that 'relatives are more entitled' (4:13), thereby superseding the earlier covenant-based rights of clients.
